---
title: "Growth rates, tables and plots"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
requireNamespace("xts", quietly = TRUE)
```

This article covers the functions that transform a series for reading
(growth rates, period-to-date totals, indexes) and those that show it
(tables and interactive plots). The examples use the package's Hawaii
data: payroll jobs (quarterly), visitor arrivals (monthly) and visitors
present (daily).

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(fcutils)
options(
  fcutils.bnk_start = as.Date("1998-01-01"),
  fcutils.bnk_end = as.Date("2035-12-31")
)
q <- conv_xts(quarterly_data_example)
jobs <- q$E_NF_HI
```

## Growth rates

`pcmp(x, lag, comp_freq)` is the percent change over `lag` periods,
compounded `comp_freq` times a year. One function covers the usual
measures for a quarterly series:

```{r}
gr <- tsbox::ts_c(
  q_q = pcmp(jobs, lag = 1),                     # quarter on quarter
  q_q_ann = pcmp(jobs, lag = 1, comp_freq = 4),  # annualized
  y_y = pcmp(jobs, lag = 4),                     # year on year
  ten_yr_ann = pcmp(jobs, lag = 40, comp_freq = 4)
)
round(tail(gr, 2), 2)
```

`pc_to_pca()` and `pca_to_pc()` convert between period and annualized
rates, and `cagr()` gives the compound annual growth rate between the first
and last observation, in percent, with the years elapsed:

```{r}
cagr(jobs[p(2015, 2024)])
```

`ma(x, order)` is a trailing moving average that includes the current
period. `index_to_base(x, base_per)` turns levels into an index that equals 100 in
the base period. A year or two dates as the base set the period's average
to 100, which makes series of different size comparable. Here total jobs
and jobs in accommodation and food services, against 2019:

```{r}
idx <- index_to_base(q[, c("E_NF_HI", "EAF_HI")], 2019)
round(idx[p(2019.4, 2020.3)], 1)
```

## Period to date

For monthly and daily data, the *to-date* functions accumulate within a
year, fiscal year (July to June), quarter or month, and compare with the
same span a year earlier.

| Function | Period | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `ytd_cum(x, avg)` | calendar year | average (or sum, `avg = FALSE`) so far |
| `ytd_gr(x)` | calendar year | % change of the year so far on a year earlier |
| `fytd_cum()`, `fytd_gr()` | fiscal year | the same for the fiscal year |
| `mtd_cum()`, `mtd_gr()` | month | the same within each month, for daily data |
| `ptd_cum(x, per)`, `ptd_gr(x, per)` | `per`: "year", "quarter", "month" | the general form |

Visitor arrivals in early 2025:

```{r}
vis <- conv_xts(monthly_data_example)$VISNS_HI
round(tail(tsbox::ts_c(
  arrivals = vis,
  ytd_avg = ytd_cum(vis),
  ytd_sum = ytd_cum(vis, avg = FALSE),
  ytd_gr = ytd_gr(vis),
  fytd_gr = fytd_gr(vis)
), 4), 1)
```

The year to March 2025 is `r round(as.numeric(ytd_gr(vis)["2025-03-01"]), 1)`%
above the same months of 2024. The fiscal year to March, which started in
July 2024, is `r round(as.numeric(fytd_gr(vis)["2025-03-01"]), 1)`% above
July 2023 to March 2024.

## Tables

`gen_table()` lays out series with their growth rates. By default the
dates run across and each series and growth rate has a row;
`time_across = FALSE` turns that around, which suits a short page.
`percent` picks the growth rate: `"pc"` (period on period), `"pcy"` (year
on year), `"pca"` (annualized) or `"none"`.

```{r}
gen_table(q[, c("E_NF_HI", "EAF_HI")],
  tbl_start = "2024-01-01", tbl_end = "2025-01-01", percent = "pcy",
  time_across = FALSE
)
```

With `save_loc`, it writes the table to a CSV file or, for `.html`, to a
searchable page.

## Interactive plots

The plot functions draw [dygraphs](https://rstudio.github.io/dygraphs/):
hover to read values, drag to zoom, and use the range selector at the
bottom. `rng_start` and `rng_end` set the initial window. All plots on a
page zoom together, so a page of plots keeps one date window; the two
plots below share 2016 to 2028.

`plot_fc()` shows up to three series, typically the forecast, an earlier
forecast and history, as lines, with the growth of the first as bars on
the right axis and a table below. This is the jobs forecast from
[Building a forecast](forecasting.html) against history:

```{r}
jobs_fc <- extend(jobs, 2025.4 ~ 1.2, 2027.4 ~ 0.8, type = "growth")
plot_fc(
  tsbox::ts_c(forecast = jobs_fc, history = jobs),
  rng_start = "2016-01-01", rng_end = "2028-01-01",
  table_start = "2024-01-01", table_end = "2028-01-01",
  width = 700
)
```

`rate = TRUE` shows the change in points instead of the percent change,
for rates such as the unemployment rate, and `yoy_gr = FALSE` shows
annualized growth instead of year on year.

`plot_1()` plots one or more series with the growth of the first, and
`plot_2ax()` puts the second series on its own axis. `plot_comp_2()` shows
several series in two panels, levels and growth. `plot_comp_3()` adds a
panel with each series indexed to 1 at `base_date`, which compares series
of different size. Accommodation and food services jobs fell much further
in 2020 than total jobs:

```{r}
plot_comp_3(q[, c("E_NF_HI", "EAF_HI")],
  base_date = "2019-10-01",
  rng_start = "2016-01-01", rng_end = "2028-01-01", width = 700
)
```

To collect many plots on one page that can be shared as a single file, put
them in a list and pass it to `save_plot_list()`.
